paragraphs: Learning language grounded in objects means connecting descriptions to what can be seen or sensed. This paper introduces a dataset that brings these signals together: objects represented through color images and depth information, accompanied by both spoken and written descriptions. It supports studying language alongside the physical information that gives it meaning.

The researchers examine differences between spoken and textual descriptions, rather than assuming they provide interchangeable language supervision. Their experiments show that the choice of modality affects learning. This matters because a system learning from written descriptions may encounter different descriptive language when people interact with it through speech.

The dataset makes it possible to investigate interactions among images, depth, text, speech, and transcriptions within a shared resource. Its contribution is particularly relevant to research connecting robotics, language processing, and human-computer interaction. The stated findings motivate paying attention both to how information is recorded and to the language people use in each modality.
neurips-2021-a-spoken-language-dataset-o.tldr: A dataset pairs object imagery and depth with spoken and written descriptions, showing that language modality affects learning.

paragraphs: Speech recognition and text-to-speech systems commonly learn from labeled recordings, making dataset quality an important part of their development. This paper examines common problems in speech data and introduces tools for constructing datasets and interactively analyzing errors. Its focus is the data work that supports supervised speech systems.

The toolbox addresses two related activities: assembling a speech dataset and exploring an existing one to investigate problems. The construction component builds on earlier work. The authors also describe the exploration component as, to their knowledge, the first open-source tool of its kind, framing that novelty claim with an explicit qualification.

The paper demonstrates the tools by creating a Russian speech dataset and analyzing Multilingual LibriSpeech and Mozilla Common Voice. These examples cover both building a resource and inspecting established collections. Released within the NeMo framework, the tools provide a reusable way to carry out dataset construction and error analysis, making those activities a concrete part of the speech research workflow.
neurips-2021-a-toolbox-for-construction-.tldr: An open-source toolbox supports speech dataset construction and interactive error analysis, with demonstrations on Russian and existing multilingual data.

paragraphs: A dataset can become influential before its origins and contents are adequately documented. This paper examines that problem through BookCorpus, which has been used to train GPT-N and BERT models. The authors describe its sparse documentation as documentation debt: missing context about motivation, composition, and collection that remains relevant after widespread adoption.

They produce a retrospective datasheet that gathers key information about the dataset and identifies deficiencies. Their investigation finds evidence of copyright restriction violations affecting many books, thousands of duplicated books, and substantial imbalance in genre representation. These findings concern distinct aspects of the resource: permission to use material, repeated content, and the distribution of its subject matter.

The authors distinguish these findings from tentative concerns, including hints that some authors contribute disproportionately. Those possibilities require further research. The resulting datasheet is an initial documentation effort and a cautionary case study showing how a widely used training resource can carry unresolved questions about its construction and composition.
neurips-2021-addressing-documentation-de.tldr: A retrospective BookCorpus datasheet finds evidence of copyright issues, extensive duplication, and genre imbalance in a widely used training dataset.

paragraphs: Data-driven simulation methods aim to complement traditional numerical methods, potentially reducing computation or learning physical models from data. Comparing these approaches is difficult when each study uses different physical problems and measures success differently. This paper introduces a benchmark suite intended to make those comparisons more systematic.

The suite includes four representative physical systems alongside classical time integrators and several kinds of learned methods. The latter include kernel-based approaches, multilayer perceptrons, convolutional neural networks, and nearest-neighbor methods. Bringing these approaches into one framework gives researchers shared problems on which to examine different strategies for simulating physical behavior.

Evaluation covers stability, accuracy, and computational efficiency, treating simulation quality as more than a single measure of prediction error. The framework is also configurable so that researchers can adapt it to other learning tasks. The contribution is a foundation for consistent evaluation and future extensions in scientific machine learning, rather than a reported universal winner among simulation methods.
neurips-2021-an-extensible-benchmark-sui.tldr: A configurable benchmark compares classical and learned physical simulation methods on stability, accuracy, and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Argoverse 2 provides three complementary datasets for studying how self-driving systems perceive their surroundings and predict movement. Its annotated Sensor Dataset contains 1,000 sequences combining imagery from seven ring cameras and two stereo cameras with lidar and map-aligned vehicle pose. Three-dimensional boxes identify objects in 26 categories, with samples supporting model training and evaluation.

The Lidar Dataset supplies 20,000 unlabeled sequences for self-supervised learning and point-cloud forecasting. The Motion Forecasting Dataset adds 250,000 scenarios selected for challenging interactions between the autonomous vehicle and other actors. Models receive histories describing location, heading, velocity, and category, and predict the future movement of designated actors.

Across all three datasets, each scenario includes a high-definition map with three-dimensional lane and crosswalk geometry. The data span six cities, connecting sensor observations and movement histories to local road structure. This collection supports multiple research tasks through related forms of driving data, and the datasets are released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.
neurips-2021-argoverse-2-next-generation.tldr: Argoverse 2 combines annotated sensors, unlabeled lidar, and motion scenarios with detailed maps for self-driving perception and forecasting research.

paragraphs: A language model can perform well on a benchmark by exploiting patterns that do not demonstrate common sense. This paper tackles benchmark construction through a game in which people write questions intended to fool a rival AI. Players earn extra points for using specified phrases, giving the designers some control over the questions collected.

The resulting CommonsenseQA 2.0 dataset contains 14,343 yes-or-no questions. The game is designed to combine participant engagement with directed data collection at scale. Questions created against one AI also prove difficult for models orders of magnitude larger, showing that the challenge extends beyond the particular opponent used during collection.

The strongest reported baseline, the 11-billion-parameter T5-based Unicorn model, reaches 70.2% accuracy. GPT-3 reaches 52.9% in a few-shot inference setup, while humans achieve 94.1%. These results establish a substantial human-model gap on this dataset. They also support the usefulness of game-based question writing for exposing weaknesses that strong performance on other benchmarks can leave hidden.
neurips-2021-commonsenseqa-2-0-exposing-.tldr: A question-writing game produces a commonsense benchmark on which tested language models remain well below human accuracy.

paragraphs: CREAK tests whether language models can combine facts about particular entities with everyday reasoning. Knowing an entity's attributes is only part of the task: a model must also infer what those attributes imply. The paper places this combination between conventional fact verification and commonsense benchmarks centered on generic situations.

The dataset contains roughly 13,000 human-written English claims labeled true or false, plus a small contrast set. Human performance is in the high nineties. The experiments focus on a closed-book setting, asking models to judge claims using their learned knowledge rather than consulting external material during the evaluation.

A baseline trained on an existing fact-verification benchmark struggles with CREAK's inferences. Training on CREAK substantially improves accuracy, but the model still falls short of human performance. This gap suggests that success at fact verification does not automatically provide the combination of entity knowledge and unstated commonsense reasoning tested here. The benchmark offers a focused way to study that combination.
neurips-2021-creak-a-dataset-for-commons.tldr: CREAK tests reasoning that combines entity facts with common sense, revealing a remaining human-model gap even after dataset-specific training.

paragraphs: Satellite data can support agricultural machine learning, but using it requires more than choosing a model. Researchers need labeled examples, familiarity with satellite products, appropriate processing, and ways to handle multidimensional geographic information. CropHarvest is introduced to reduce these barriers and make satellite-based research more accessible to the machine learning community.

The dataset contains more than 90,000 geographically diverse samples with agricultural labels. It is accompanied by a Python package, providing both a collection of labeled data and software intended to facilitate its use. The paper's contribution centers on making this kind of research resource available across a broad set of locations.

The motivating challenges include changes in data across geography, meaning, and time, together with highly uneven label frequencies. These issues make agricultural remote sensing a useful setting for studying how models handle varied data. The authors also point to potential societal applications in food security and climate change, positioning CropHarvest as enabling infrastructure for research toward those goals.
neurips-2021-cropharvest-a-global-datase.tldr: CropHarvest provides over 90,000 geographically diverse agricultural samples and a Python package to lower barriers to satellite-based machine learning.

paragraphs: Strong language-understanding results often come from benchmarks that supply substantial amounts of labeled training data. This paper asks how well models learn when only a small number of examples are available. It introduces CLUES to address the lack of standardized evaluation in this few-shot setting, where differing experimental choices make studies difficult to compare.

The reported experiments show a large gap from human performance on most tasks when labeled examples are scarce, even though recent models can match humans with abundant supervision. The authors also observe differences among model families and adaptation techniques. Few-shot evaluation therefore reveals distinctions that performance under generous training conditions may obscure.

Beyond supplying tasks, the paper discusses principles for evaluating true few-shot learning and proposes a unified experimental approach. That emphasis matters because the conditions under which models are adapted are part of what the benchmark measures. CLUES provides public code and data intended to support comparable research on learning new language-understanding tasks from limited examples.
neurips-2021-few-shot-learning-evaluatio.tldr: CLUES standardizes few-shot language-understanding evaluation and reveals large gaps from human performance on most tasks with limited labeled data.

paragraphs: Generating a readable medical report from images raises two connected evaluation problems: explaining the report's findings and assessing its quality reliably. The authors argue that existing benchmarks provide insufficient explanatory annotations and that ordinary language-generation metrics alone make comparisons between medical reports unreliable. FFA-IR is designed to address both issues.

The benchmark pairs 1,048,584 fundus fluorescein angiography images from clinical practice with 10,790 reports. It includes annotations organized around 46 lesion categories and provides English and Chinese reports for every case. The lesion annotations add structured medical information to the image-report pairs, supporting research that connects generated descriptions with explainable findings.

For evaluation, the authors propose nine human assessment criteria alongside widely used language-generation metrics. This broadens the benchmark's approach beyond judging generated text through those automatic measures alone. FFA-IR is presented as a testbed for more explainable and reliable report generation; its anticipated contribution to clinical and medical-imaging research is a goal, rather than an established deployment outcome.
neurips-2021-ffa-ir-towards-an-explainab.tldr: FFA-IR combines bilingual medical reports, lesion annotations, and human evaluation criteria to support more explainable and reliable report-generation research.

paragraphs: HM3D supplies 1,000 building-scale reconstructions of real indoor environments, including residences and stores. Each environment is a textured three-dimensional mesh. Its 112,500 square meters of navigable space provide a large collection of settings for training agents that learn to move through virtual representations of physical places.

The paper reports advantages over the comparison datasets in scale, visual fidelity, and reconstruction completeness. Navigable area is 1.4–3.7 times larger than MP3D and Gibson. Across the stated photorealistic dataset comparisons, rendered images have 20–85% higher fidelity relative to real camera images, and meshes have 34–91% fewer artifacts associated with incomplete surface reconstruction.

These dataset improvements accompany strong PointGoal navigation results. In the reported comparisons, agents trained on HM3D perform best whether tested on HM3D, Gibson, or MP3D. They also reach 100% performance on Gibson-test, prompting the authors to suggest retiring that episode dataset. The findings concern this navigation task and these evaluations, supporting HM3D's usefulness for training and testing embodied agents.
neurips-2021-habitat-matterport-3d-datas.tldr: HM3D offers 1,000 detailed indoor reconstructions and yields the strongest reported PointGoal navigation results across three evaluation datasets.

paragraphs: Machine learning studies using intensive-care time series can be hard to compare even when researchers have access to shared raw datasets. Different choices of prediction tasks and preprocessing create different experimental problems. This paper introduces a benchmark based on HiRID to bring more consistency to the development and comparison of ICU models.

The authors define multiple clinically relevant tasks in collaboration with clinicians. They also provide a reproducible pipeline that constructs both the model inputs and the labels used for learning and evaluation. Standardizing these steps helps researchers compare methods within a common setup instead of having each publication independently define how raw observations become a prediction task.

The paper analyzes leading sequence-modeling approaches and reports limitations of deep learning methods for this type of data. Its central contribution combines clinically informed task design with reproducible data preparation and model assessment. The intended benefit is a fairer basis for comparing research across a broad spectrum of ICU-related tasks.
neurips-2021-hirid-icu-benchmark-a-compr.tldr: The HiRID benchmark standardizes clinically informed ICU tasks and data preparation to enable more comparable evaluations of sequence models.

paragraphs: Mapping land cover from high-resolution remote-sensing images requires assigning categories to image pixels. A model that works in one landscape may transfer poorly to another, particularly between urban and rural areas. LoveDA is designed to study both accurate segmentation and this transfer problem, which can hinder mapping at city or national scale.

The dataset contains 5,987 images and 166,768 annotated objects from three cities. Its urban and rural domains introduce variation in object scale, background complexity, and class frequencies. These properties make it suitable for studying ordinary land-cover segmentation as well as unsupervised domain adaptation, where researchers examine transfer between domains without target-domain label supervision.

The authors benchmark eleven segmentation methods and eight adaptation methods. They also explore multiscale architectures and strategies, additional background supervision, and pseudo-label analysis as responses to the dataset's challenges. The contribution is a shared testbed that makes transferability an explicit part of land-cover research alongside learning useful visual representations.
neurips-2021-loveda-a-remote-sensing-lan.tldr: LoveDA benchmarks land-cover segmentation and transfer between urban and rural imagery with different scales, backgrounds, and class distributions.

paragraphs: Multimodal models combine different sources of information, but research across application areas can be difficult to compare. MultiBench brings 15 datasets, 10 modalities, 20 prediction tasks, and six research areas into a unified benchmark. Its automated pipeline standardizes data loading, experiment setup, and evaluation, reducing differences in how methods are tested.

The benchmark evaluates generalization, training and inference costs, and robustness when modalities are noisy or missing. It also provides standardized implementations of 20 approaches covering different ways to combine information, define learning objectives, and train models. This makes predictive performance one part of a broader assessment that includes resource demands and imperfect inputs.

The authors report that applying approaches from other research areas improves state-of-the-art performance on nine of the fifteen datasets. That result suggests useful methods were separated by research boundaries. MultiBench creates a common setting for transferring those ideas while highlighting remaining challenges in scaling multimodal learning and handling realistic data imperfections.
neurips-2021-multibench-multiscale-bench.tldr: MultiBench unifies multimodal evaluation across datasets and tasks, assessing prediction quality, computational costs, and resilience to missing or noisy inputs.

paragraphs: Conversational assistants need to identify what a person wants and extract the details needed to fulfill that request. These activities are called intent detection and slot filling. This paper questions whether impressive scores on standard benchmarks demonstrate that models can handle the variations found in realistic spoken language.

NATURE is a collection of simple transformations applied to evaluation utterances. The transformations introduce spoken-language variation while preserving the utterance's meaning. This creates a focused robustness test: the requested interpretation remains the same, while the wording changes in ways intended to reflect human speech. The benchmark examples therefore test more than success on their original phrasing.

Applying these transformations to common intent-detection and slot-filling benchmarks significantly reduces the performance of the tested models, with accuracy drops of up to 40%. This is a reported upper extent of degradation, not a uniform effect across all evaluations. The findings show that meaning-preserving language variation can reveal weaknesses hidden by strong results on unchanged benchmark test sets.
neurips-2021-nature-natural-auxiliary-te.tldr: NATURE exposes conversational models' sensitivity to meaning-preserving spoken-language variations, with reported accuracy drops of up to 40%.

paragraphs: OmniPrint is a tool for generating synthetic images of individual printed characters for machine learning research. Inspired by established character and digit datasets, it makes the production of examples configurable. Researchers can vary the characters' languages, fonts, styles, and distortions when constructing a dataset for a particular study.

The generator includes 935 fonts covering 27 scripts, along with many distortion types. These options let dataset creation incorporate several sources of visual variation within the same tool. Its basic unit is an isolated printed character, so the contribution concerns generating character examples with controlled appearance rather than describing a collection of complete documents.

The paper presents several proof-of-concept uses, including a meta-learning dataset designed for the MetaDL competition. This illustrates how the generator can support research setups that require newly assembled character data. The stated contribution is the available synthesis tool and demonstrations of its use, providing a configurable resource for building printed-character learning problems.
neurips-2021-omniprint-a-configurable-pr.tldr: OmniPrint generates configurable images of isolated printed characters using 935 fonts across 27 scripts and customizable distortions.

paragraphs: Python Programming Puzzles defines each challenge through a short verification program. The solver must find an input that makes that program return true. Because the verifier specifies the task and checks the answer, evaluation requires neither a reference solution nor natural-language interpretation of a problem statement.

The released P3 dataset spans simple string tasks, classic puzzles, competitive-programming problems, and longstanding algorithmic or mathematical problems. The authors build enumerative, GPT-3, and Codex solvers that can learn from their own previous solutions without access to reference answers. This connects automatically checkable tasks with a way to accumulate useful solved examples.

Codex performs best in the reported experiments, solving up to 18% of 397 test problems with one attempt and 80% with 1,000 attempts per problem. The attempt budget is therefore essential to interpreting those results. A small user study also finds positive correlations between coding experience and success, and between human and AI difficulty. These findings suggest potential relevance to broader program-synthesis research.
neurips-2021-programming-puzzles-a28b3df.tldr: P3 evaluates program synthesis through executable Python puzzles whose solutions can be checked directly without reference answers.

paragraphs: Robotics benchmarks face a practical tension: identical hardware and objects support reproducibility, but strict setup requirements limit participation. More flexible protocols are easier to adopt, yet differences between laboratories complicate comparisons. RB2 addresses this tension by including algorithm implementations alongside the usual tasks and experimental procedures.

Researchers can run the supplied methods in their own laboratory and compare a new approach against locally reproduced baselines. Because these local rankings may differ across setups, RB2 also provides a mechanism for pooling experimental data into a global ranking. The comparison therefore incorporates evidence from multiple laboratories rather than assuming their raw performance numbers are directly interchangeable.

The benchmark uses tasks inspired by the Southampton Hand Assessment Procedures and was run in two laboratories. In those experiments, simple open-loop behavior cloning outperforms more complicated approaches, including closed-loop models, recurrent networks, and offline reinforcement learning. These findings challenge expectations within the tested settings and illustrate why reproducible baseline implementations are useful for assessing algorithmic progress.
neurips-2021-rb2-robotic-manipulation-be.tldr: RB2 combines reproducible local baselines with pooled rankings to compare manipulation algorithms across different robotic setups.

paragraphs: Benchmark datasets help organize machine learning research by giving communities shared problems and measures of progress. This paper studies how those resources are actually used and reused. It examines differences among research communities and changes over the period from 2015 to 2020, treating dataset adoption itself as an object of investigation.

The authors find that individual task communities increasingly concentrate on fewer datasets. They also observe substantial use of datasets originally associated with other tasks. Together, these patterns show both concentration around common resources and movement of resources across research boundaries, revealing how benchmark use changes beyond the setting in which a dataset first appeared.

Across the field, usage is also concentrated on datasets introduced by researchers at a small number of elite institutions. The authors identify implications for scientific evaluation, AI ethics, and equity and access. The study makes clear that benchmark choices are part of the organization of research: they influence which shared resources become central to evaluating progress.
neurips-2021-reduced-reused-and-recycled.tldr: An analysis of dataset use finds growing concentration, substantial reuse across tasks, and field-wide reliance on datasets from a few elite institutions.

paragraphs: Neural MMO is a research platform for studying many agents acting over long periods in open-ended environments. It combines large populations, extended time horizons, open-ended tasks, and modular game systems. The authors present this combination as its distinctive contribution, noting that earlier environments include subsets of these properties.

The platform is designed to be computationally accessible and is released as free, open-source software. Documentation and tools for training, logging, and visualization accompany the environment. These resources support researchers in adapting to a setting where learning involves sustained interaction among large numbers of agents rather than only isolated decision makers.

Initial baseline experiments show that agents trained in large populations explore more and acquire a progression of skills. These observations provide early evidence about learning in the platform. More difficult problems, including cooperation among many teams, remain open research questions that Neural MMO is intended to support. The paper also discusses platform limitations, possible mitigations, and continued development.
neurips-2021-the-neural-mmo-platform-for.tldr: Neural MMO supports large-population, long-horizon agent research, with initial experiments showing increased exploration and progressive skill learning.

paragraphs: Therapeutics Data Commons organizes machine learning problems across drug discovery and development into a shared platform. The paper emphasizes that progress requires meaningful task definitions and carefully curated data. Its described release contains 66 datasets across 22 learning tasks, giving researchers a common entry point into a broad range of therapeutics problems.

The platform also supplies data-processing functions, multiple ways to split datasets, systematic evaluation strategies, molecule-generation oracles, and public leaderboards. These resources are integrated through an open Python library. Combining datasets with evaluation tools helps connect access to data with the practical work of developing and assessing models.

Experiments on selected datasets show that even the strongest tested algorithms struggle with important challenges. These include shifts in data distributions, learning across scales and modalities, and generalizing reliably to unfamiliar examples. TDC therefore provides both research infrastructure and evidence of remaining gaps. Faster model development and eventual biomedical or clinical translation are the authors' aspirations for the platform.
neurips-2021-therapeutics-data-commons-m.tldr: TDC unifies therapeutics datasets and evaluation tools while documenting persistent challenges in distribution shift and generalization.

paragraphs: Timers and Such is an open-source dataset of spoken English commands for everyday voice-control uses involving numbers. The paper identifies a gap in existing spoken-language-understanding datasets and builds a benchmark around this practical category of requests. Numerical content is central to the commands the resource is designed to represent.

The authors describe how the dataset was designed and created, then use it to experiment with several baseline models. These include approaches based on automatic speech recognition and end-to-end approaches. Including both families gives researchers a common dataset on which to investigate different ways of turning speech into an understood command.

The baseline code is available through the SpeechBrain toolkit, pairing the data contribution with reusable implementations. This makes the benchmark a concrete starting point for experiments on number-bearing voice commands. The paper's stated contribution is the dataset, its construction, and baseline experimentation, establishing a shared setting for studying this part of spoken-language understanding.
neurips-2021-timers-and-such-a-practical.tldr: Timers and Such benchmarks spoken English commands involving numbers and provides speech-recognition-based and end-to-end baseline implementations.

paragraphs: One-shot image segmentation assigns pixel labels for a target category using a single example image and its mask. Many methods first train on other categories, then are evaluated on categories excluded from that training. This paper investigates how the training data can introduce biases that undermine performance in this setting.

The authors present evidence for two biases. Class Negative Bias arises when non-target objects are treated as background during training. Salience Bias affects accuracy on target pixels that are less visually prominent. They report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art results when these biases are eliminated, highlighting the importance of how training examples and labels are constructed.

The paper also argues that existing benchmark scores do not adequately match real-world expectations. It introduces Tiered One-shot Segmentation, built from PASCAL 5i and FSS-1000, with evaluation metrics for each tier. Experiments on several methods aim to make accuracy reporting more uniform while revealing finer distinctions in where a method may be applicable.
neurips-2021-what-ails-one-shot-image-se.tldr: The paper identifies two data-induced segmentation biases and introduces tiered evaluation to reveal differences obscured by existing benchmark scores.

paragraphs: Agents trained to maximize reward in environments that ignore moral concerns may learn harmful behavior. This paper creates a richer setting for investigating that problem through Jiminy Cricket, a suite of 25 text adventure games containing thousands of morally significant scenarios. The goal is to evaluate behavior in situations with substantial language and semantic complexity.

The environments include dense annotations for every possible action, enabling evaluation of moral behavior alongside reward-seeking performance. This provides a way to distinguish progress within a game from the moral character of the actions used to achieve it. The benchmark expands the scope beyond the small settings emphasized in earlier work.

The authors also develop an artificial conscience approach that uses commonsense moral knowledge from language models to influence agent actions. Their experiments find that this approach can steer agents toward more moral behavior without sacrificing performance. The result demonstrates compatibility between these objectives in the evaluated settings, while the suite provides a resource for further research on morally guided agents.
neurips-2021-what-would-jiminy-cricket-d.tldr: Jiminy Cricket evaluates moral behavior in text adventures, where an artificial conscience can improve tested agents' conduct without reducing performance.

paragraphs: Forecasting wildfire spread requires data that connects fire behavior with the conditions surrounding it. The paper identifies a shortage of comprehensive linked data as an obstacle to building forecasting models. WildfireDB addresses that obstacle by bringing historical fire information together with relevant variables, including weather, vegetation, and topography.

The open-source dataset contains more than 17 million data points describing fire spread across the continental United States over the decade covered by the study. The authors explain the algorithmic process used to prepare and integrate the information. This integration is central to the contribution because the intended models need fire observations connected to potentially relevant surrounding conditions.

The paper also presents benchmark results for learned wildfire-spread forecasting models. These experiments accompany the dataset with an initial basis for studying prediction using the integrated data. WildfireDB is positioned as infrastructure for data-driven fire-spread research, with fire risk management providing the practical motivation for making these connected observations available.
neurips-2021-wildfiredb-an-open-source-d.tldr: WildfireDB links over 17 million fire-spread observations with environmental variables to support data-driven forecasting research.
